topics.title: Forces, Resultant Force, and Inertia
topics.summary: A force is a vector measured in newtons representing a push or pull. Newton's first law states that an object remains at rest or at constant velocity unless acted on by a resultant force.
key_points: Forces have size and direction, making them vectors measured in newtons.
The resultant force is the single force equivalent to all forces acting together.
Inertia is the tendency of an object to resist changes in motion, which increases with mass.
Balanced forces produce a resultant force of zero.

questions.prompt: What is the single force called that has the same effect as all forces acting together on an object?
hints: Think about combining multiple forces into one overall effect.
It results from combining all individual forces.
The term starts with 'result'.
questions.explanation: The material defines resultant force as the single force with the same effect as all forces acting together.
questions.key_point: The resultant force is the single force equivalent to all forces acting together.

questions.prompt: Why are forces classified as vectors?
options: They have both size and direction
They are measured only in kilograms
They only act on stationary objects
They always cancel each other out
questions.answer: They have both size and direction
hints: Consider what information is required to fully describe a force.
Vectors have two main properties, unlike scalars.
Forces have magnitude and a specific way they point.
questions.explanation: Forces have both size and direction, which makes them vectors.
questions.key_point: Forces have size and direction, making them vectors measured in newtons.

questions.prompt: What happens when forces acting on an object are balanced?
options: The mass of the object decreases
The resultant force equals the object's weight
hints: Think about what 'balanced' means for opposing forces.
Opposing forces of equal magnitude cancel out.
The net or combined force becomes zero.
questions.explanation: Balanced forces have equal and opposite effects, meaning their resultant force is zero.
questions.key_point: Balanced forces produce a resultant force of zero.

questions.prompt: Why does a passenger lurch forward when a bus suddenly brakes?
options: Their inertia causes their body to resist the change in velocity
A forward resultant force pushes their body ahead
The bus's mass suddenly transfers to the passenger
Air resistance inside the bus pushes them forward
questions.answer: Their inertia causes their body to resist the change in velocity
hints: Think about what property makes objects keep doing what they were doing.
The passenger was already moving and resists changing that motion.
This is an example of Newton's first law and inertia.
questions.explanation: Due to inertia, the passenger's body tends to maintain its previous velocity when the bus slows down.
questions.key_point: Inertia is the tendency of an object to resist changes in motion, which increases with mass.

questions.prompt: How does increasing an object's mass affect its inertia?
options: It has no effect on its inertia
hints: Consider whether heavier objects are harder or easier to accelerate.
Greater mass means more resistance to changing motion.
More mass directly leads to more inertia.
questions.explanation: Inertia is directly related to mass; having more mass means an object has more inertia.
questions.key_point: Inertia is the tendency of an object to resist changes in motion, which increases with mass.

questions.prompt: If an object is moving at a constant velocity, what can be inferred about the forces acting on it?
options: There is a non-zero resultant force
A forward resultant force is speeding it up
Only friction is acting on the object
hints: Recall Newton's first law regarding constant velocity.
If velocity does not change, no overall net force is acting.
The resultant force must be zero, meaning forces are balanced.
questions.explanation: According to Newton's first law, an object stays at constant velocity when the resultant force is zero (forces are balanced).
questions.key_point: Balanced forces produce a resultant force of zero.

questions.prompt: Forces have size and direction, so they are ____ measured in newtons.
hints: This term describes any quantity with magnitude and direction.
It contrasts with scalars.
It starts with the letter 'v'.
questions.explanation: Because forces possess both magnitude (size) and direction, they are categorized as vectors.
questions.key_point: Forces have size and direction, making them vectors measured in newtons.

questions.prompt: The tendency of an object to resist changes to its motion is called ____ .
hints: This concept is central to Newton's first law of motion.
It increases with an object's mass.
The word begins with 'in-'.
questions.explanation: Inertia is defined as the natural tendency of any object to resist changes in its state of motion.
questions.key_point: Inertia is the tendency of an object to resist changes in motion, which increases with mass.

questions.prompt: When all forces acting on an object cancel out, the ____ force is zero.
hints: This refers to the single overall force combining all acting forces.
When forces are balanced, this overall force is zero.
It starts with 'r'.
questions.explanation: Balanced forces cancel each other completely, producing a resultant force of zero.
questions.key_point: The resultant force is the single force equivalent to all forces acting together.

questions.prompt: A box is pulled to the right with 15 N and to the left with 15 N. What is the motion of the box if it was initially stationary?
options: It moves at increasing speed to the left
It moves at constant velocity to the right
hints: Calculate the resultant force acting on the box.
15 N right minus 15 N left gives a resultant force of zero.
An object at rest stays at rest when forces are balanced.
questions.explanation: The opposing 15 N forces balance out, giving a resultant force of zero. By Newton's first law, a stationary object remains at rest.
questions.key_point: Balanced forces produce a resultant force of zero.

questions.prompt: A 1000 kg car and a 50 kg cart are both at rest. Which requires a larger resultant force to achieve the same change in motion, and why?
options: The car, because it has greater mass and therefore more inertia
The cart, because smaller masses resist motion changes more
Both require the same force because they are both at rest
The car, because its resultant force is naturally zero
questions.answer: The car, because it has greater mass and therefore more inertia
hints: Consider how mass affects an object's resistance to changing motion.
More mass means more inertia.
A greater inertia requires a greater force to produce the same change.
questions.explanation: Because the car has a larger mass, it has significantly more inertia and resists changes to its motion more than the lighter cart.
questions.key_point: Inertia is the tendency of an object to resist changes in motion, which increases with mass.

questions.prompt: A space probe drifts in deep space far from any gravitational forces at 500 m/s. What will happen to its velocity if no forces act on it?
options: It will continue moving at 500 m/s in a straight line
It will gradually slow down to a complete stop
It will speed up because there is no friction
Its direction will randomly change over time
questions.answer: It will continue moving at 500 m/s in a straight line
hints: Apply Newton's first law of motion.
No resultant force is acting on the probe.
Without a resultant force, constant velocity is maintained.
questions.explanation: Without any resultant force acting on it, an object in motion maintains its constant velocity according to Newton's first law.
questions.key_point: The resultant force is the single force equivalent to all forces acting together.

topics.title: Newton's Second and Third Laws
topics.summary: Newton's second law relates resultant force to mass and acceleration through the equation F = m a. The third law states that interacting objects exert equal and opposite forces of the same type on each other.
key_points: Resultant force equals mass multiplied by acceleration (F = m a).
Doubling the resultant force doubles acceleration, while doubling mass halves it.
When object A exerts a force on object B, B exerts an equal and opposite force on A.
Action-reaction pairs act on different objects and therefore do not cancel.

questions.prompt: According to Newton's second law, what does resultant force equal?
hints: Look at the formula F = m a.
Recall the terms represented by m and a.
F is force, m is mass, and a is acceleration.
questions.explanation: Newton's second law defines resultant force as mass multiplied by acceleration (F = m a).
questions.key_point: Resultant force equals mass multiplied by acceleration (F = m a).

questions.prompt: What happens to an object's acceleration if the resultant force acting on it is doubled?
hints: Acceleration is directly proportional to resultant force.
Consider the formula a = F / m.
Multiplying F by 2 multiplies a by 2.
questions.explanation: Acceleration is proportional to resultant force, so doubling the force doubles the acceleration.
questions.key_point: Doubling the resultant force doubles acceleration, while doubling mass halves it.

questions.prompt: What does Newton's third law state about object A exerting a force on object B?
options: Object B exerts an equal and opposite force on object A
Object B exerts a smaller force in the same direction on object A
Object A cancels out all forces acting on object B
Object B experiences zero net force from object A
questions.answer: Object B exerts an equal and opposite force on object A
hints: This law describes action and reaction pairs.
Forces in interaction pairs are equal in magnitude.
The direction of the reaction force is opposite to the action force.
questions.explanation: Newton's third law states that if object A exerts a force on object B, B exerts an equal and opposite force on A.
questions.key_point: When object A exerts a force on object B, B exerts an equal and opposite force on A.

questions.prompt: Why do action-reaction force pairs never cancel each other out?
options: They act in the same direction
They are of different types of forces
hints: Forces can only cancel if they act on the same body.
Think about where each force of the pair is applied.
One force acts on object A, while the other acts on object B.
questions.explanation: Action and reaction forces act on two separate objects, so they cannot cancel each other.
questions.key_point: Action-reaction pairs act on different objects and therefore do not cancel.

questions.prompt: If you apply the same resultant force to an object with twice the mass, how does the acceleration change?
hints: Acceleration is inversely proportional to mass.
Look at the formula a = F / m.
Doubling the denominator halves the value of acceleration.
questions.explanation: From a = F / m, doubling the mass while keeping force constant halves the acceleration.
questions.key_point: Doubling the resultant force doubles acceleration, while doubling mass halves it.

questions.prompt: A swimmer pushes backwards against the water. According to Newton's third law, what propels the swimmer forward?
options: The water pushing forward on the swimmer
A decrease in the swimmer's mass
questions.answer: The water pushing forward on the swimmer
hints: Identify the interaction pair.
The swimmer exerts a force on the water.
The water exerts an equal and opposite reaction force on the swimmer.
questions.explanation: By Newton's third law, the water exerts an equal and opposite forward force on the swimmer.
questions.key_point: When object A exerts a force on object B, B exerts an equal and opposite force on A.

questions.prompt: Resultant force is calculated by multiplying mass by ____ .
hints: Recall the formula F = m a.
The symbol 'a' stands for this quantity.
It measures the rate of change of velocity.
questions.explanation: Newton's second law is F = m a, where resultant force equals mass multiplied by acceleration.
questions.key_point: Resultant force equals mass multiplied by acceleration (F = m a).

questions.prompt: Doubling an object's mass causes its acceleration under a constant resultant force to be ____ .
hints: Acceleration is inversely proportional to mass.
Increasing mass makes it harder to accelerate.
2 times the mass results in 1/2 the acceleration.
questions.explanation: Since a = F / m, doubling the mass halves the resulting acceleration.
questions.key_point: Doubling the resultant force doubles acceleration, while doubling mass halves it.

questions.prompt: Action and reaction pairs do not cancel because they act on ____ objects.
hints: Forces only balance if applied to the same object.
Consider whether the two forces act on one body or two bodies.
Object A acts on B, and B acts on A.
questions.explanation: Action-reaction forces do not cancel because they act on different objects rather than the same one.
questions.key_point: Action-reaction pairs act on different objects and therefore do not cancel.

questions.prompt: A resultant force of 12 N acts on a 4 kg cart. What is the acceleration of the cart?
hints: Use the formula a = F / m.
Divide the force by the mass.
Compute 12 divided by 4.
questions.explanation: Using a = F / m, acceleration = 12 N / 4 kg = 3 m/s^2.
questions.key_point: Resultant force equals mass multiplied by acceleration (F = m a).

questions.prompt: A rocket engine expels hot exhaust gases downwards. What is the reaction force according to Newton's third law?
options: The gases pushing the rocket upwards
Air resistance pushing against the rocket
The rocket pulling the Earth upwards
questions.answer: The gases pushing the rocket upwards
hints: Identify the two objects interacting: rocket and exhaust gas.
The action is rocket pushing gas downwards.
The reaction is gas pushing rocket in the opposite direction.
questions.explanation: When the rocket exerts a downward force on the gas, the gas exerts an equal and opposite upward force on the rocket.
questions.key_point: When object A exerts a force on object B, B exerts an equal and opposite force on A.

questions.prompt: A cart's mass is doubled while the resultant force acting on it is also doubled. How does its new acceleration compare to the original?
hints: Doubling force doubles acceleration.
Doubling mass halves acceleration.
Consider the combined effect of (2 * F) / (2 * m).
questions.explanation: Doubling force doubles acceleration, but doubling mass halves it, resulting in the same acceleration.
questions.key_point: Doubling the resultant force doubles acceleration, while doubling mass halves it.

topics.title: Weight, Friction, and Terminal Velocity
topics.summary: Weight is the product of mass and gravitational field strength, while friction and air resistance oppose motion. A falling object reaches terminal velocity when opposing air resistance balances its downward weight.
key_points: Weight is calculated as mass multiplied by gravitational field strength (W = m g).
Friction and air resistance act against the direction of an object's motion.
Terminal velocity is reached when air resistance equals weight, resulting in balanced forces.
Opening a parachute increases air resistance, which lowers the terminal velocity.

questions.prompt: How is an object's weight calculated according to Newton's laws and mechanics?
options: Mass multiplied by gravitational field strength
Mass multiplied by acceleration due to friction
Resultant force divided by gravitational field strength
questions.answer: Mass multiplied by gravitational field strength
hints: Recall the formula W = m g.
Consider what 'm' and 'g' represent in the equation for weight.
Weight is the product of mass and the strength of the local gravitational field.
questions.explanation: Weight is given by the formula W = m g, which is mass multiplied by gravitational field strength.
questions.key_point: Weight is calculated as mass multiplied by gravitational field strength (W = m g).

questions.prompt: In which direction do friction and air resistance act on a moving object?
options: In the same direction as motion
Perpendicular to the direction of motion
hints: These forces oppose movement.
Think about what resistive forces do to motion.
They push or pull opposite to the object's travel direction.
questions.explanation: Friction and air resistance always act against the direction of an object's motion.
questions.key_point: Friction and air resistance act against the direction of an object's motion.

questions.prompt: What happens to a falling object when the upward air resistance equals its downward weight?
options: It comes to an immediate stop
hints: The forces on the falling object become balanced.
When resultant force is zero, velocity remains constant.
This maximum steady speed is called terminal velocity.
questions.explanation: When upward air resistance matches weight, forces balance and the object reaches terminal velocity.
questions.key_point: Terminal velocity is reached when air resistance equals weight, resulting in balanced forces.

questions.prompt: Why does a skydiver stop accelerating once they reach terminal velocity?
options: Air resistance balances weight, so the resultant force is zero
Gravity stops acting on the skydiver at high speeds
The skydiver's mass decreases as they fall
Air resistance becomes much greater than the skydiver's weight
questions.answer: Air resistance balances weight, so the resultant force is zero
hints: Think about Newton's first law and balanced forces.
Acceleration requires a non-zero resultant force.
At terminal velocity, the upward drag matches downward gravitational pull.
questions.explanation: When air resistance equals weight, the resultant force becomes zero, meaning acceleration stops and velocity stays constant.
questions.key_point: Terminal velocity is reached when air resistance equals weight, resulting in balanced forces.

questions.prompt: Why does opening a parachute cause a skydiver to fall at a lower terminal velocity?
options: It increases air resistance, balancing weight at a slower speed
It reduces the skydiver's total weight
It changes the direction of the gravitational field
questions.answer: It increases air resistance, balancing weight at a slower speed
hints: Consider the effect of a parachute on drag.
A larger surface area creates more air resistance for a given speed.
Because drag increases, balance occurs at a lower speed.
questions.explanation: Opening a parachute greatly increases air resistance, so upward drag equals downward weight at a much lower speed.
questions.key_point: Opening a parachute increases air resistance, which lowers the terminal velocity.

questions.prompt: A car moves horizontally forward on a flat road. Which force acts directly backwards against its motion?
hints: Identify the resistive contact force.
Weight acts vertically downwards, not backwards.
Resistive forces such as friction act opposite to the direction of travel.
questions.explanation: Friction acts against the forward direction of motion, opposing the car's movement.
questions.key_point: Friction and air resistance act against the direction of an object's motion.

questions.prompt: Weight is calculated by multiplying mass by ____ field strength.
hints: It is the field that gives rise to the 'g' in W = m g.
This field is caused by Earth's gravity.
The term starts with 'grav-'
questions.explanation: Weight is defined by W = m g, where g represents gravitational field strength.
questions.key_point: Weight is calculated as mass multiplied by gravitational field strength (W = m g).

questions.prompt: A falling object reaches ____ velocity when the upward air resistance equals its downward weight.
hints: It is the final, steady speed of a falling object.
The word starts with 't'.
It refers to the constant velocity reached when forces are balanced.
questions.explanation: Terminal velocity is the steady speed reached when opposing drag balances the downward pull of weight.
questions.key_point: Terminal velocity is reached when air resistance equals weight, resulting in balanced forces.

questions.prompt: Opening a parachute increases air resistance, resulting in a ____ terminal velocity.
hints: Parachutes are used to make landing safer and slower.
More air resistance means you do not need to fall as fast to balance weight.
Does terminal velocity become higher or lower?
questions.explanation: A parachute increases air resistance, allowing weight to be balanced at a much lower terminal velocity.
questions.key_point: Opening a parachute increases air resistance, which lowers the terminal velocity.

questions.prompt: An astronaut with a mass of 80 kg stands on a planet where g = 4 N/kg. What is their weight?
hints: Use the formula W = m g.
Multiply the mass (80 kg) by the gravitational field strength (4 N/kg).
80 times 4 equals 320.
questions.explanation: Using W = m g, Weight = 80 kg × 4 N/kg = 320 N.
questions.key_point: Weight is calculated as mass multiplied by gravitational field strength (W = m g).

questions.prompt: A 500 N skydiver is falling at terminal velocity. What is the magnitude of the air resistance acting on them?
hints: At terminal velocity, the forces are balanced.
The downward force is the skydiver's weight of 500 N.
The upward air resistance must exactly balance the downward weight.
questions.explanation: At terminal velocity, the forces are balanced, meaning air resistance equals weight (500 N).
questions.key_point: Terminal velocity is reached when air resistance equals weight, resulting in balanced forces.

questions.prompt: A crate slides to the right across a warehouse floor. What is the direction of the frictional force acting on the crate?
hints: Friction opposes the direction of motion.
The crate is moving horizontally to the right.
The opposing direction to right is left.
questions.explanation: Because friction acts against the direction of motion, it acts to the left when an object moves to the right.
questions.key_point: Friction and air resistance act against the direction of an object's motion.
